solvers.record_7_reasoning:
Record 7 names gw-prod-02 (on roster) and its Authorization header is well formed ('GW-HMAC-SHA256 keyId=gw-prod-02, signature=' prefix), so it gets past the first three checks and comes down to the signature. Under the frozen scheme its canonical string is: GET 
 /v2/ledger/export 
 tag=%7e&tag=z&verbose= 
 content-type:application/json
host:gw.example.com
x-gw-date:2025-11-20T16:02:41Z
x-gw-key-id:gw-prod-02 
 content-type;host;x-gw-date;x-gw-key-id 
 e3b0c442...b855 (sha256 of empty, body absent), no trailing LF. HMAC with the 32-byte gw-prod-02 key does not equal the presented b3135a25..., so it is rejected/signature-mismatch. I checked why with node: the presented signature reproduces exactly under the rules in force on its x-gw-date, 2025-11-20: query ordered by name then percent-decoded value (tag=z before tag=%7e, since '~' sorts after 'z'), valueless parameter bare ('verbose', the 11-04 trial), signed set x-gw-* plus content-type only (no host), body field UNSIGNED, trailing LF, ';' separator, stripped key. So it is a genuinely valid signature under an earlier form of the rules, and 12-2025-12-09-rollout.md [Cutover] says 'There is no grace period ... a request signed under any earlier form of the rules is rejected as a mismatch'. The record exercises 5 rules at once (query order, valueless parameter, signed set, body hash, terminator); an implementation left on any stale combination of them could wrongly verify it. The evidence line still carries the frozen-scheme signature and canonical_sha256, with reason signature-mismatch.
solvers.how_i_read: Read in full: instruction.md, 01-decision-register.md, src/pipeline.ts, tsconfig.json, requests/sample-requests.json, all 5 capture files, the 3 key files (od -c), 02-2025-09-30-kickoff.md, and appendices 22, 23, 24. For session notes 03 to 12 I did not read linearly: I listed all section headings with counts, classed the repetitive operational headings (Capacity, Load test, Proxy upgrade, replay/queue/runbook/cutover etc) as filler, and extracted every remaining section for every signer with a node script, then read that extract (about 140 items) in full, tracing each of the 12 rules through the dates including 'in line with X as it stands today' references and corrections. Appendix 25 read in full minus blanks; appendices 20, 21, 26, 27 only by their bullet lines and header. I also grepped all dossier files for the inbound aliases, 'key file', 'line ending', 'SDK 3.3'. Filler sections in 03-12 and in 20/21/26/27 were not read sentence by sentence, so a decision hidden inside a filler-headed section would have been missed unless it used an inbound alias (the grep would have caught that). Then I simulated the scheme in node (scratch files in C:/expert/migrate-legacy-api-signing-to-a-typescript-evidence-pipeline/runs/frontier-review/solver-1/: ex.js, sim.js, dec.txt) and brute-forced rule combinations against the signatures in records 6 and 7.
solvers.hardest_part: Two things. First, the indirections: three GW rules turn on a correction that moves an item between signers (header values gains inner-collapse via a correction of an item minuted under callback signing; the ',' separator and the 11-11 always-hash item are taken away by corrections, one of them under a heading called just 'Minutes'), one on a cross-reference to another signer's state on a given day (query order on 11-11), and three on conditions resolved by a single bullet line in an appendix (sign-off register, proxy captures, release calendar). Each is easy alone; the risk is missing one of roughly ten among ~230KB of near-identical filler and five signers written under 3-4 aliases each. Second, key bytes: nothing in the dossier says whether the GW signer strips the key file's line ending, and the strace cannot show it. I only got it from the sample signatures.
solvers.anything_ambiguous:
1) key_bytes is the one I think is not derivable from the documents. The instruction says the strace and lsof settle 'how it read them', but the strace only shows a 33-byte read including '\n'; it does not show what was passed to HMAC. Every key-file decision in the dossier is for another signer (and they go both ways), and the existing port uses the whole file. A careful reader could defensibly keep the whole file. Only checking record 6 (and the old-rule reconstruction of record 7) shows the key is the 32 bytes without the LF. An agent that does not test against record 6 gets every signature wrong while having all 11 canonicalisation rules right. Exactly what to strip (one LF, CRLF, all trailing whitespace) is also unstated.
2) Key id value handling: GW-034 says the value is used verbatim, while header values are trimmed/collapsed in the canonical block. For a key id sent with padding, readers could disagree on whether lookup and the evidence key_id use the raw or the normalised value.
3) Duplicate header names, and whether authorization is the only exclusion when compared case-insensitively (I assume lowercased name === 'authorization'), are not spelled out. Sort tie-break for equal names is unspecified.
4) Empty query segments ('a=1&&b', trailing '&') and a target ending in '?' are unspecified.
5) 'Whatever follows signature= ... apart from surrounding whitespace': I trim and compare case-sensitively to lowercase hex; an uppercase-hex correct signature would be a mismatch under 'compared as is'.
6) Body hashing encoding: body is a JSON string, I assume UTF-8 bytes.
I did not open any forbidden path. I wrote only scratch files under runs/frontier-review/solver-1/.

solvers.record_7_reasoning:
Record 7 names gw-prod-02 (on the roster) and carries a well formed Authorization header (exact prefix 'GW-HMAC-SHA256 keyId=gw-prod-02, signature='), so it passes the first three checks and comes down to the signature. Under the frozen rules its canonical string is: GET / /v2/ledger/export / tag=%7e&tag=z&verbose= / content-type:application/json, host:gw.example.com, x-gw-date:2025-11-20T16:02:41Z, x-gw-key-id:gw-prod-02 / content-type;host;x-gw-date;x-gw-key-id / e3b0c442...b855, with no trailing LF. HMAC with the LF-stripped gw-prod-02 key gives 8049639f...33a5, which is not the presented b3135a25...f6c8, so the outcome is rejected/signature-mismatch with the recomputed signature in the evidence.

I then brute-forced the historical rule variants with node to see what the presented signature is. It reproduces exactly under the rules in force on the record's own X-GW-Date, 2025-11-20: values percent-decoded for ordering (so tag=z sorts before tag=%7e, i.e. '~'), valueless parameter written bare ('verbose', the 11-04 trial), signed set x-gw-* plus content-type (the 11-18 stopgap, so host is left out), UNSIGNED token for an absent body, trailing LF after the sixth field, ';' separator, stripped key. So it is a genuine signature made under an earlier form of the scheme, not a corrupted one. 12-2025-12-09-rollout.md '## Cutover' says there is no grace period and a request signed under any earlier form is rejected as a mismatch, which confirms the outcome. The record exercises four frozen rules at once: raw-byte value ordering ('%' 0x25 sorts before 'z'), escape case left as %7e, trailing '=' on verbose, and all headers signed. The pipeline must not look at X-GW-Date to pick a rule set.
solvers.how_i_read: Read in full: instruction.md, captures (README, both lsof, both strace), src/pipeline.ts, tsconfig.json, sample-requests.json, the three key files via od, 01-decision-register.md, 02-2025-09-30-kickoff.md, and appendices 20 (release calendar), 22 (sign-off register), 23 (proxy captures). After the kickoff showed that most of each note is repeated operational filler, I wrote a node script (scratch at C:/expert/migrate-legacy-api-signing-to-a-typescript-evidence-pipeline/runs/frontier-review/solver2/filt.js) that normalises names, numbers, hosts, partners and services and drops any sentence whose template appears 8 or more times across the dossier, then read everything that survived for 03 to 12 and for appendices 21, 24, 25, 26, 27. So those files were read through a filter, not line by line. I backed it with greps over all dossier files for every GW alias (GW-HMAC, inbound request, partner request, gateway request scheme), for SDK 3.3 / general availability, and for key file / line ending / gw-prod. Then computed canonical strings and HMACs with node (sig.js) and brute-forced 2,592 rule combinations per record against the presented signatures of records 6 and 7 (brute.js). No forbidden path was opened; scratch files are only under runs/frontier-review/solver2/.
solvers.hardest_part: Tracking GW state through the corrections. Three of them move a decision between signers after the fact: 11-11 moves the 11-04 header-value collapse INTO GW from callback signing (easy to miss, because a search for GW aliases in the 11-04 note does not find it), 11-18 moves the 11-11 body-hash item OUT of GW, and 12-02 moves the 11-25 ',' separator OUT of GW. On top of that there are five aliases per signer, conditional items resolved only in appendices (signed header set via the sign-off register, escape case via the proxy captures, dot segments via the release calendar), trials, parked proposals, and an 'in line with batch manifest signing as it stands today' cross-reference. The second hard part is the key bytes: nothing written says the Perl signer drops the line ending, and I only got there by testing record 6.
solvers.anything_ambiguous:
1. key_bytes is the one rule I could not ground in a passage. The strace shows a 33-byte read including the LF; the instruction says the captures settle 'how it read them', which a reader could defensibly take as 'whole file' (also what the starter code does). Only the sample signature in record 6 shows the LF is stripped. A solver who does not use record 6 as an oracle would fail every signature while having every documented rule right. How much to strip (one LF, CRLF, all trailing whitespace) is also open; all three shipped files are 32 bytes plus LF.
2. Key id lookup versus header value treatment: is the roster lookup and the evidence key_id the raw x-gw-key-id value (GW-034 'verbatim') or the trimmed one? A padded key id like ' gw-prod-01 ' would be unknown-key-id on my reading and signed on another. Same question for the keyId comparison inside Authorization.
3. Duplicate header names and duplicate name/value query pairs: tie order is not specified (I would use a stable sort). Whether multiple Authorization headers or a differently cased 'authorization' name matter is also unstated; I treat the name case-insensitively and take the first.
4. canonical_sha256 for missing-key-id and unknown-key-id records: the instruction says only signature is empty, so I would still compute it, but it is not said outright.
5. 'Surrounding whitespace' on the presented signature: trimmed how (spaces and tabs only, or any whitespace), and is the comparison case-sensitive against lowercase hex? I would trim all whitespace and compare exactly, so an uppercase-hex signature is a mismatch.
6. The unmet-condition items: the 10-21 escape-case item has no explicit fallback clause, unlike the 10-14 BX item ('If not, what is in place now stays'). I read unmet as no change.
7. Minor: body present but null in JSON, non-string bodies, and empty query segments ('a&&b', trailing '&') are not covered.
I am confident in 11 of the 12 rules and in all 8 outcomes, given that record 6 verifies exactly under my reading. I did not read sessions 03 to 12 unfiltered, so a GW decision phrased in a sentence template that repeats 8 or more times would have been dropped by my filter; the alias grep over the unfiltered files found nothing extra.

audits.verdict:
No fairness blocker found in the rule histories. For all 10 rules the rollout-day form is uniquely determined from the instruction and dossier: every correction points at exactly one item, every alias is in the kickoff note, both conditions have one stated outcome, SDK 3.3 has one date, the export-signer alignment has one answer, the support tickets are dated and consistent, and the register is never left contradicting a final rule. The expected hashes for the sample and all 3 holdouts reproduce from analysis/scheme.mjs, and record 7 comes out signature-mismatch.

The weakness is on the other side: less of the intended cross-document difficulty is load-bearing than the design claims. Sample record 6 settles the separator and terminator outright (chains-1). The body-hash correction and the export-signer alignment are both overwritten by later self-contained items (chains-2). The freeze note pre-resolves the SDK 3.3 item and names the sign-off appendix (chains-3). By reading alone, only 3 things can still sink an agent: the header-value correction, the escapes condition, and the path release date. Worth tightening before running models if the corrections and the alignment are meant to discriminate; none of it makes a correct agent fail.

findings.claim: The hard variant's tell is still here. The migrated scheme's events carry hand-written lead, tail and reason sentences; the other signers' are drawn from 3 leads per subject, 5 tails and 5 reasons. Blanking names, numbers and aliases and counting sentence frequency separates them, and it resolves all 3 corrections of minutes without reading one.
findings.evidence:
Command: node runs/frontier-review/shortcut/tells.mjs. It blanks people, the 5 partners, the 20 aliases, x-??-* prefixes, tokens and digits, splits into sentences, and counts each blanked sentence across the 11 notes. A one-off is a sentence occurring once that does not carry the signer name.

Output over the 125 decision passages:
- oneoff>=1: migrated 17/22, other 10/103
- oneoff>=2: migrated 13/22, other 0/103
- oneoff>=3: migrated 3/22, other 0/103
- len: migrated median 318, mean 325.4, max 475; others median 229, mean 229.6, max 374
- len>=360: 8 migrated / 1 other
- len>=400: 4 migrated / 0 other

The crossed items fall exactly on the tell:
- header_values-2025-11-04-set (minuted under the webhook signer, really the migrated scheme's): trueGW=true shownGW=false oneoff=3 len=409
- body_hash-2025-11-11-set (minuted under the migrated scheme, really the export signer's): shownGW=true oneoff=0
- names_join-2025-11-25-set (really the mesh signer's): shownGW=true oneoff=0

Procedure that reads no correction (node runs/frontier-review/shortcut/tellproc.mjs): keep passages naming the migrated scheme, drop its 'set' passages with 0 one-off sentences, add any other signer's passage with >=2 one-offs. Output: 'ADDED: labelled for another signer but has >=2 one-off sentences' for exactly the 2025-11-04 folded item; 'DROPPED' for the 2025-11-11 always-sha256 and 2025-11-25 comma items (and the superseded 2025-10-14 trimmed). State before conditionals is wrong only on signed_headers; after the one '5 of 5' conditional: {"sample":true,"h1":true,"h2":true,"h3":true}.

Cause in build.mjs: the GW add() calls pass lead/tail/reason, e.g. lead: "D. Achterberg reran the comparison between what clients send and what arrives. ...", tail: "SDK 3.2 already behaves this way.", while render() does `const lead = e.lead ?? fillNames(pick(dim.leads)); const tail = e.tail ?? fillNames(pick(TAILS)); const reason = e.reason ?? pick(REASONS);`. The mis-minuted export and mesh items have no lead or tail, so they render as "Northwind hit failures on requests that carry no body. ... No change for anyone else." and "Umbrella asked how the signed header names are separated. ... P. Oyelaran will update the client notes."

findings.suggested_fix: In build.mjs make lead, tail and reason come from one source for every signer. Either (a) delete the lead/tail/reason fields from the GW add() calls and move those sentences into DIMS[dim].leads, TAILS and REASONS with {person}/{partner} slots so any signer can draw them, or (b) give each decoy event its own written 2-sentence lead and tail from a per-subject bank at least as large as the number of decoy events on that subject, drawn without replacement, so decoys have the same share of one-off sentences. Either way give the 2 mis-minuted decoy items (BX body_hash 2025-11-11, MS names_join 2025-11-25) the same treatment as a real GW item. Add a build-time guard next to the needle check: recompute the blanked-sentence frequency table and passage lengths, and throw if any threshold on one-off count or length selects migrated-scheme passages with precision above about 0.5, or if the 3 crossed items differ from their label-mates on either measure.

findings.claim: The 2 signed sample records work as oracles. Output:
- record 6: 2700 of 25920 settings reproduce the presented signature. trailing_newline: PINNED -> none; names_join: PINNED -> semicolon; key_bytes: PINNED -> newline-stripped; everything else free.
- record 7: 18 of 25920 settings reproduce it. query_order: PINNED -> name-then-decoded-value; signed_headers: PINNED -> x-gw-plus-content-type; trailing_newline: PINNED -> lf; percent_escapes: PINNED -> as-received; valueless_parameter: PINNED -> bare; names_join: PINNED -> semicolon; key_bytes: PINNED -> newline-stripped.

Record 6 in sample-requests.json has 2 signed headers, "X-GW-Key-Id" and "X-GW-Date": "2025-12-08T09:14:03Z", so the separator shows in the signature. Record 7's target is "/v2/ledger/export?tag=%7e&tag=z&verbose"; the lowercase %7e is what pins the escape rule.

Record 7 also hands the agent the state on 2025-11-20 for 6 rules, a ground truth to check its reading of the minutes against. The instruction invites this: "what the gateway checks is the scheme as it stood on that day".
findings.suggested_fix: In build.mjs give `fresh` one signed header only, so the separator never appears in its canonical string: headers: [["X-GW-Key-Id", "gw-prod-01"]], with the date moved into the body or the path. In `stale`, uppercase the escape (target "/v2/ledger/export?tag=%7E&tag=z&verbose"): '~' still sorts after 'z' decoded and '%' before it raw, so decoded ordering is still exercised but percent_escapes becomes free; and cut it to one signed x-gw header plus content-type only if names_join should stay unpinned there too. Add a guard that brute-forces everySetting() against both signatures, as oracle.mjs does, and throws if names_join or percent_escapes is pinned by either record.

findings.claim: Of the cross-document steps the design counts on, only one changes the graded state. Ignoring the alignment with the export signer, the body-hash correction and both appendix lookups for 'effective with' and the failed condition costs nothing; with S2, ignoring the names_join correction costs nothing either. That leaves the header_values correction as the single load-bearing step.
findings.evidence:
Command: node runs/frontier-review/shortcut/lastwins.mjs. L1 skips every align and correction and gets body_hash and query_order right; its only errors are 'header_values=trimmed; percent_escapes=uppercased; path=dot-segments-resolved; names_join=comma'. L2 (never apply a conditional or an 'effective with' item) fixes escapes and path with no appendix opened.

Why each one is dead weight:
- Alignment: ANSWER-KEY.md lists '2025-11-11, align, with BX, which had name-then-decoded-value' then '2025-11-25, set, name-then-value'. The explicit set a fortnight later overwrites it, so the export signer's history never has to be read. The aligned value is also stated under the migrated scheme's own alias in 25-partner-support-escalations.md: "Support advised that for GW-HMAC-SHA256 query parameters are ordered by name and then by value, with each value percent-decoded before it is compared."
- Body-hash correction: the mis-minuted export item sets 'always' on 2025-11-11 and the migrated scheme's real decision on 2025-12-02 sets the same value ('2025-12-02, set, always'), so an agent that never sees the correction lands on the right rule.
- names_join correction: pinned by sample record 6 (S2).
- Proxy condition and SDK 3.3: the default "If not, what is in place now stays for this cutover" / "Until SDK 3.3 is generally available, what is in place now stays" is the right answer for both, so doing nothing is correct.
findings.suggested_fix: In the event table in build.mjs: (1) make the alignment the last adopting event on its subject. For example move the explicit name-then-value decision to the export signer's history at an earlier date and have GW align with BX after it, and remove ["2025-11-13", "Globex", "query_order"] from gwTickets so the result is not restated under a GW alias. (2) Make the mis-minuted export body-hash item carry a value the migrated scheme does not end on, or date it after GW's last real body-hash decision (minuted under GW at the freeze, corrected at rollout), so ignoring the correction gives a wrong rule. (3) Add an ablation guard beside the existing rollout check: replay GW with each device switched off in turn (corrections ignored, aligns ignored, every conditional treated as failed, every conditional treated as met, every 'later' ignored, every 'later' applied) and throw unless each ablation changes at least one rule of the rollout state.

audits.verdict: Not ready. Naive grep plus last-wins fails (3/10, 6/10, 7/10 rules depending on how much of the frame is read), so the cheapest dumb route is closed. Fix S1 before running any model; S2-S4 decide whether the intended difficulty is real once S1 is closed.

Both fact lines open with a migrated-scheme alias, and both are in manifest.json.

Computation: I reran node runs/frontier-review/shortcut/l3.mjs.
- With the alias-grep appendix lines and file 20 never opened: rules right 10/10, graded sets {"sample":true,"h1":true,"h2":true,"h3":true}.
- Session notes only: 9/10, wrong signed_headers=x-gw-plus-content-type, and all 4 graded sets fail.
oracle.mjs grades against the real sample and tests/holdout sets by sha256 of the reference output.

Structural claim holds:
- ANSWER-KEY.md gives path as "later, dots-collapsed, effective with SDK 3.3, 2026-01-13" and percent escapes as "condition proxy is false". Both land on the register default, so appendices 20 and 23 never change a graded rule.
- 20-release-calendar.md:5 ("SDK 3.3: general availability 2026-01-13.") is made redundant by the freeze sentence about SDK 3.3.
- Only the sign-off line in appendix 22 decides anything, and the freeze note names that register.

Caveats that bear on severity, not truth:
- The claim that all-but-authorization is "inferable" from the rollout decline is suggestive only; a careful agent would still want the register.
- Finding alias-led lines by grep is close to the intended reading path. The agent still has to match "tabled 2025-12-02" to the conditional item and handle the 3 corrections, which l3.mjs does with explicit logic.
- So this is a real reduction of the intended two-document difficulty (1 of 3 appendix lookups is load-bearing and it is signposted), not a bypass of the dossier replay. "should-fix" is reasonable; it is not a blocker.
